ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Measures of general attitudes toward a subject were coded here where items referenced usefulness or importance and excluded otherwise.

> Thirty-five samples were randomized at the level of the individual and 17 at the level of the cluster (13 by class, three by school and one by teacher); the cluster-randomized samples contribute 134 effect sizes.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Publication year also did not moderate effect sizes, F(1, 50) = 0.62, p = .433, suggesting no clear evidence of time-lag or disseminationrelated patterns.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p ≤ .020", Text = "Moderation by motivational construct is robust; it is significant at every setting of the intraclass, concurrent-outcome and longitudinal correlations (p ≤ .020) and under the dispersion adjustment (p < .001)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1364 columns across 104 data files.
#### Issues Identified

90 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 104 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 6 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  6 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
-  0 of 1 script ran without error when executed (5 more are run by another script with `source()`).
-  11 installable dependencies detected.
- 2 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 46 reported tests matched (0%).

live_data_statements: Measures of general attitudes toward a subject were coded here where items referenced usefulness or importance and excluded otherwise.

Thirty-five samples were randomized at the level of the individual and 17 at the level of the cluster (13 by class, three by school and one by teacher); the cluster-randomized samples contribute 134 effect sizes.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 6 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:6, File = c("01_prepare_effect_sizes.R", 
"02_vmatrix_model.R", "03_figures.R", "04_sensitivity_extras.R", 
"05_rob2_standard.R", "00_run_all.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—", "—", "01_prepare_effect_sizes.R, 02_vmatrix_model.R, 03_figures.R, 04_sensitivity_extras.R, 05_rob2_standard.R"
), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", 
"dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `Final Data Sheet STEM Meta 2026 V17.xlsx` to `../Final Data Sheet STEM Meta 2026 V17.xlsx` (in 01_prepare_effect_sizes.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file. **13 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 5 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("01_prepare_effect_sizes.R", "02_vmatrix_model.R", 
"03_figures.R", "04_sensitivity_extras.R", "05_rob2_standard.R", 
"00_run_all.R"), Outcome = c("run_by_source", "run_by_source", 
"run_by_source", "run_by_source", "run_by_source", "errored"), 
    Detail = c("", "", "", "", "", "runtime"), "Time (s)" = c(0, 
    0, 0, 0, 0, 0.6)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "00_run_all.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "(non-literal)"), row.names = c(NA, -1L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

2 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
**Run by another script**

5 scripts are run by another script with `source()`, so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("01_prepare_effect_sizes.R", "02_vmatrix_model.R", 
"03_figures.R", "04_sensitivity_extras.R", "05_rob2_standard.R"
```

text.text: Students' motivation in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) often declines across schooling, with implications for continued STEM participation.
Psychosocial interventions offer a promising approach to improving STEM motivation, yet their overall effectiveness and variation across motivational outcomes remain unclear.

Drawing on situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT) as an integrating framework, this three-level meta-analysis synthesized 348 effect sizes from 52 independent samples of randomized controlled trials.
Results revealed a small but significant positive overall effect on STEM motivation (g = 0.12, 95% CI [0.06, 0.17]).

Effects differed significantly across motivational outcomes, with the largest effects observed for task value (g = 0.18) and mindset (g = 0.16), followed by interest (g = 0.10) and competence beliefs (g = 0.09).
Effects on achievement goals (g = 0.09, six samples) and perceived cost (g = 0.04) were not statistically significant.
Intervention type, sample gender composition, and the proportion of participants from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM were not significant moderators.
Longer interventions and in-person or mixed delivery, relative to online, were associated with larger effects, but only the duration association remained significant after a dispersion adjustment.
Bayesian selection models provided strong evidence against p-value-based publication selection, and the overall effect remained significant after excluding samples at high risk of bias.
Overall, these findings suggest that psychosocial interventions can modestly improve students' STEM motivation, particularly task value and mindset.
Future research should examine whether these motivational gains can be sustained over time and translated into longer-term STEM engagement and participation.

Innovations in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) are reshaping the skills required to participate in modern societies, and education systems face increasing pressure to equip students with scientific and technological skills (Holmes et al., 2022; World Economic Forum, 2025; Zhou & Shirazi, 2025).
text.formatted: Innovations in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) are reshaping the skills required to participate in modern societies, and education systems face increasing pressure to equip students with scientific and technological skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Holmes et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">World Economic Forum, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">Zhou & Shirazi, 2025</ref>).

text.text: Yet participation and persistence in STEM pathways remain low.

In U.S. tertiary education (i.e., postsecondary education, including universities, colleges, and other institutions offering degrees or equivalent qualifications), fewer than one-third of undergraduates declare a STEM major and fewer than one-quarter complete a STEM degree (Abramenko & Nadzan, 2024).
text.formatted: In U.S. tertiary education (i.e., postsecondary education, including universities, colleges, and other institutions offering degrees or equivalent qualifications), fewer than one-third of undergraduates declare a STEM major and fewer than one-quarter complete a STEM degree <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Abramenko & Nadzan, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Participation is also unequal.

Enrollment among girls and women remains lower than their academic achievement would predict (Stoet & Geary, 2018), and comparable patterns are observed among students from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM (hereafter URM students).
text.formatted: Enrollment among girls and women remains lower than their academic achievement would predict <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">(Stoet & Geary, 2018)</ref>, and comparable patterns are observed among students from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM (hereafter URM students).

text.text: In the United States, 25% of URM students initially declare a STEM major but are less likely than their White peers to complete it (Abramenko & Nadzan, 2024; Mau, 2016).
text.formatted: In the United States, 25% of URM students initially declare a STEM major but are less likely than their White peers to complete it <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Abramenko & Nadzan, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Mau, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Here, participation refers to enrollment in STEM coursework or programs, and persistence to continued enrollment once enrolled.
Motivational processes are central to students' decisions to enter, persist in, or withdraw from STEM pathways (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: Motivational processes are central to students' decisions to enter, persist in, or withdraw from STEM pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Competence beliefs, perceived task value and a sense of belonging shape engagement and persistence (Blatt et al., 2020; Cheryan et al., 2017; Harackiewicz et al., 2023; Master et al., 2017), particularly in STEM, where learning environments are often highly evaluative (Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018).
text.formatted: Competence beliefs, perceived task value and a sense of belonging shape engagement and persistence <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Blatt et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Cheryan et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Harackiewicz et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Master et al., 2017)</ref>, particularly in STEM, where learning environments are often highly evaluative <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Efforts to improve STEM participation therefore increasingly target these motivational processes, particularly for groups historically underrepresented in STEM.

One approach is psychosocial (or "wise") interventions, which are brief, theoretically grounded strategies that change how students interpret themselves and their academic experiences rather than what they are taught (Yeager & Dweck, 2012; Yeager & Walton, 2011).
text.formatted: One approach is psychosocial (or "wise") interventions, which are brief, theoretically grounded strategies that change how students interpret themselves and their academic experiences rather than what they are taught <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">(Yeager & Dweck, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">Yeager & Walton, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The present meta-analysis synthesizes such interventions in STEM, restricting inclusion to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to strengthen causal inference.
Previous meta-analytic evidence indicates that randomized studies of educational motivation interventions yield smaller average effects than quasi-experimental studies (Lazowski & Hulleman, 2016).
text.formatted: Previous meta-analytic evidence indicates that randomized studies of educational motivation interventions yield smaller average effects than quasi-experimental studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(Lazowski & Hulleman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The overarching aim of this study is to estimate the effects of psychosocial interventions on students' STEM motivation and examine whether these effects vary across intervention types, motivational outcomes, and sample composition, specifically the proportions of girls and women and of students from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM.
Psychosocial interventions operate by introducing a social factor ("social") to shape students' motivational processes ("psycho") (Yeager & Walton, 2011).
text.formatted: Psychosocial interventions operate by introducing a social factor ("social") to shape students' motivational processes ("psycho") <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Yeager & Walton, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Motivation refers to the internal processes that energize, direct, and sustain goal-directed behavior (Reeve, 2025; Ryan & Deci, 2020).
text.formatted: Motivation refers to the internal processes that energize, direct, and sustain goal-directed behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Reeve, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Ryan & Deci, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These processes arise from individuals' physical and psychological needs (Bong et al., 2023) and from students' continual appraisals of how interesting, useful and identity-relevant an activity is, which determine how much effort and persistence they invest.
text.formatted: These processes arise from individuals' physical and psychological needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Bong et al., 2023)</ref> and from students' continual appraisals of how interesting, useful and identity-relevant an activity is, which determine how much effort and persistence they invest.

text.text: Motivational constructs have evolved alongside the development of motivation theory.

Research has progressed from early drive and achievement-motive accounts through cognitive perspectives emphasizing expectancies, attributions, and goals, to contemporary frameworks highlighting the situated and socially embedded nature of motivational beliefs (Ford, 1992; Graham, 2020; Graham & Weiner, 2012).
text.formatted: Research has progressed from early drive and achievement-motive accounts through cognitive perspectives emphasizing expectancies, attributions, and goals, to contemporary frameworks highlighting the situated and socially embedded nature of motivational beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Ford, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Graham, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Graham & Weiner, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The conceptual boundaries among constructs have also evolved.
For example, perceived cost, originally conceptualized as a component of subjective task value, has received increasingly distinct conceptualization and measurement.
As discussed by Koenka (2020), motivational theories encompass related but conceptually distinguishable constructs whose operationalizations may overlap in empirical research.
text.formatted: As discussed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Koenka (2020)</ref>, motivational theories encompass related but conceptually distinguishable constructs whose operationalizations may overlap in empirical research.

text.text: This historical development is relevant to the present synthesis because studies may define and measure nominally similar constructs differently, and our construct categories necessarily accommodate some of this variation.

Psychosocial interventions in STEM draw on several theoretical traditions, and the trials synthesized here retain the grounding their authors gave them: utility-value interventions are framed within expectancyvalue theory, growth-mindset interventions within implicit theories of ability, and attributional retraining within attribution theory.

The present review keeps that grounding rather than recasting every construct in the terms of one theory, and uses situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT; Eccles & Wigfield, 2020 , 2024) as an integrating framework to relate these traditions and interpret the findings.
text.formatted: The present review keeps that grounding rather than recasting every construct in the terms of one theory, and uses situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Eccles & Wigfield, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref> as an integrating framework to relate these traditions and interpret the findings.

text.text: SEVT suits this role because it places students' interpretations of experience, goals and identities upstream of the expectancies and values that guide achievement-related choices, and because it emphasizes how these beliefs are shaped by social, cultural, developmental and immediate learning contexts.
The review does not test the contextual processes the theory proposes.

SEVT has its origins in Atkinson's (1957) early motivation model, which identified motive, expectancy and incentive as determinants of behavior, and in the expectancy-value theory (EVT) of Eccles et al. (1983), which became a dominant account of how individuals form achievement-related choices.
text.formatted: SEVT has its origins in <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Atkinson's (1957)</ref> early motivation model, which identified motive, expectancy and incentive as determinants of behavior, and in the expectancy-value theory (EVT) of <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Eccles et al. (1983)</ref>, which became a dominant account of how individuals form achievement-related choices.

text.text: SEVT builds on EVT by more explicitly emphasizing the situated and dynamic nature of motivational beliefs.

Although both frameworks identify expectancies for success and subjective task values as central determinants of achievement-related choices, SEVT places greater emphasis on how these beliefs develop and change through interactions among students' prior experiences, socialization processes, cultural contexts, and immediate learning environments (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020 , 2024).
text.formatted: Although both frameworks identify expectancies for success and subjective task values as central determinants of achievement-related choices, SEVT places greater emphasis on how these beliefs develop and change through interactions among students' prior experiences, socialization processes, cultural contexts, and immediate learning environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: SEVT comprises two broad components, one psychological and one concerned with socialization.

The psychological component comprises the beliefs that directly guide achievement-related choices (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024): expectancies for success and subjective task values, which encompass intrinsic value (interest and enjoyment), attainment value (identity relevance, the importance of doing well for one's sense of self), utility value (perceived usefulness) and cost, what must be given up or endured to participate, such as effort, lost alternatives or negative emotions (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: The psychological component comprises the beliefs that directly guide achievement-related choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024)</ref>: expectancies for success and subjective task values, which encompass intrinsic value (interest and enjoyment), attainment value (identity relevance, the importance of doing well for one's sense of self), utility value (perceived usefulness) and cost, what must be given up or endured to participate, such as effort, lost alternatives or negative emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The socialization component comprises the contextual influences that shape these beliefs over time, including family background, prior achievement, ethnicity, and exposure to gender roles and stereotypes (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: The socialization component comprises the contextual influences that shape these beliefs over time, including family background, prior achievement, ethnicity, and exposure to gender roles and stereotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Students' decisions to engage with, persist in, or withdraw from STEM therefore reflect both their expectancies and values and the sociocultural environments that shape them (Kirkham et al., 2023; Murphy et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Students' decisions to engage with, persist in, or withdraw from STEM therefore reflect both their expectancies and values and the sociocultural environments that shape them <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Kirkham et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Murphy et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Alongside SEVT, several theoretical traditions inform the motivational constructs examined in this review.

Self-determination theory (SDT) emphasizes the roles of autonomy, competence, and relatedness in motivation and distinguishes intrinsic motivation as engagement in an activity for its inherent interest or enjoyment (Ryan & Deci, 2002 , 2017; Ryan & Vansteenkiste, 2023).
text.formatted: Self-determination theory (SDT) emphasizes the roles of autonomy, competence, and relatedness in motivation and distinguishes intrinsic motivation as engagement in an activity for its inherent interest or enjoyment <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">(Ryan & Deci, 2002</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Ryan & Vansteenkiste, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Social cognitive theory emphasizes self-efficacy, or beliefs about one's capability to perform specific actions, in explaining effort and persistence (Bandura, 2023; Schunk & DiBenedetto, 2020).
text.formatted: Social cognitive theory emphasizes self-efficacy, or beliefs about one's capability to perform specific actions, in explaining effort and persistence <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Bandura, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Schunk & DiBenedetto, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Attribution theory concerns how students explain their successes and failures (Weiner, 1985), whereas implicit theories of ability distinguish beliefs that ability can be developed (growth mindset) from beliefs that it is fixed (Dweck, 2006).
text.formatted: Attribution theory concerns how students explain their successes and failures <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">(Weiner, 1985)</ref>, whereas implicit theories of ability distinguish beliefs that ability can be developed (growth mindset) from beliefs that it is fixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Dweck, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Achievement goal theory examines the purposes students pursue in achievement settings, distinguishing mastery goals, focused on learning and improvement, from performance goals, focused on demonstrating competence relative to others, each with approach and avoidance forms (Elliot, 2023; Elliot & McGregor, 2001; Elliot & Sommet, 2023).
text.formatted: Achievement goal theory examines the purposes students pursue in achievement settings, distinguishing mastery goals, focused on learning and improvement, from performance goals, focused on demonstrating competence relative to others, each with approach and avoidance forms <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Elliot, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Elliot & McGregor, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Elliot & Sommet, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These traditions address related aspects of motivation but define distinct constructs.

For example, self-efficacy, academic self-concept, and perceived competence are conceptually related to the ability beliefs and expectancies emphasized in SEVT, while interest and intrinsic motivation overlap with its intrinsic value component.

Attributions, mindset, and achievement goals address different aspects of motivation, including explanations for success and failure, beliefs about the malleability of ability, and purposes for achievement.

Across these traditions, psychosocial interventions seek to reshape how students interpret academic experiences, particularly those involving challenge, uncertainty, or evaluation (Yeager & Walton, 2011).
text.formatted: Across these traditions, psychosocial interventions seek to reshape how students interpret academic experiences, particularly those involving challenge, uncertainty, or evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Yeager & Walton, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These interpretations are particularly salient in STEM, where demanding content and evaluative feedback are common, and reshaping them may improve engagement, persistence, and performance (Rosenzweig & Wigfield, 2016), potentially with greater benefits for students experiencing belonging uncertainty or stereotype threat (Harackiewicz et al., 2016).
text.formatted: These interpretations are particularly salient in STEM, where demanding content and evaluative feedback are common, and reshaping them may improve engagement, persistence, and performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Rosenzweig & Wigfield, 2016)</ref>, potentially with greater benefits for students experiencing belonging uncertainty or stereotype threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Harackiewicz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Psychosocial interventions are defined here as targeted activities that primarily aim to change how students interpret themselves, their schooling or a subject, such as the relevance of course content, the meaning of difficulty or their sense of belonging (Walton & Wilson, 2018; Yeager & Walton, 2011).
text.formatted: Psychosocial interventions are defined here as targeted activities that primarily aim to change how students interpret themselves, their schooling or a subject, such as the relevance of course content, the meaning of difficulty or their sense of belonging <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Walton & Wilson, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">Yeager & Walton, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: They are distinguished from instructional interventions by their primary target, students' beliefs and interpretations rather than what is taught or how, although they may be embedded in regular instruction or combined with changes to teaching materials or practice.

Most psychosocial interventions fall into three broad categories that target distinct but interrelated processes: task value, framing, and personal values interventions (Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018).
text.formatted: Most psychosocial interventions fall into three broad categories that target distinct but interrelated processes: task value, framing, and personal values interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: importance, usefulness and relevance of a topic (Gaspard et al., 2017; Rosenzweig & Wigfield, 2016).
text.formatted: importance, usefulness and relevance of a topic <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Gaspard et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Rosenzweig & Wigfield, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Typically through writing or reflection, students articulate how STEM content is meaningful or useful to their goals, interests or everyday lives, which strengthens their willingness to engage, particularly when the content first seems abstract or irrelevant (Hulleman et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Typically through writing or reflection, students articulate how STEM content is meaningful or useful to their goals, interests or everyday lives, which strengthens their willingness to engage, particularly when the content first seems abstract or irrelevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Hulleman et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: They are among the most widely tested psychosocial approaches in RCTs (Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018).
text.formatted: They are among the most widely tested psychosocial approaches in RCTs <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Students who attribute poor performance to a lack of intelligence may read setbacks as fixed indicators of low ability and disengage (Hamm et al., 2020); framing interventions present challenges as normal, manageable opportunities for learning, and promote attributions to controllable factors such as effort or strategy, so that students persist in rather than avoid demanding STEM tasks (Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018).
text.formatted: Students who attribute poor performance to a lack of intelligence may read setbacks as fixed indicators of low ability and disengage <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Hamm et al., 2020)</ref>; framing interventions present challenges as normal, manageable opportunities for learning, and promote attributions to controllable factors such as effort or strategy, so that students persist in rather than avoid demanding STEM tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Personal values interventions address students' identity, self-worth and belonging (Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018).
text.formatted: Personal values interventions address students' identity, self-worth and belonging <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Value-affirmation exercises invite students to reflect on personally meaningful values, which can buffer stereotype threat and self-doubt in evaluative contexts (Falco & Summers, 2019).
text.formatted: Value-affirmation exercises invite students to reflect on personally meaningful values, which can buffer stereotype threat and self-doubt in evaluative contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Falco & Summers, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Exposure to relatable role models can show that success in STEM is compatible with one's identity and goals (González-Pérez et al., 2020; Stout et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Exposure to relatable role models can show that success in STEM is compatible with one's identity and goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(González-Pérez et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Stout et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Psychosocial interventions commonly involve brief activities, although their intensity varies considerably.

In the included studies, interventions ranged from a single application, in 10 studies, to repeated activities across several weeks or a term, such as 13 weekly sessions or 20 sessions over four weeks (Supplemental Table S4).
text.formatted: In the included studies, interventions ranged from a single application, in 10 studies, to repeated activities across several weeks or a term, such as 13 weekly sessions or 20 sessions over four weeks (Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Interventions are frequently delivered during regular instruction or through online platforms, with motivational outcomes assessed primarily through student self-reports at the end of the intervention or academic term.
Evaluations typically randomize students or classrooms to intervention and comparison conditions, often using neutral writing or reflection activities as controls.
Follow-up beyond the academic term is uncommon, limiting evidence about the durability of intervention effects.
To organize the motivational outcomes measured across included studies, the present review specifies seven categories: competence, interest, task value, cost, goals, mindset, and attributions.

Participation, persistence and career intentions (stated plans for future STEM study or work) are choices that motivation is expected to shape; they were treated as outcomes of motivation rather than as motivational beliefs and were not coded.
For the meta-analysis, motivational outcomes were grouped according to the content of the measures rather than solely by their theoretical origins.

This approach was adopted because primary studies do not consistently distinguish related constructs, and finer classifications would leave some categories with too few samples for meaningful analysis.
The classification was informed by Rosenzweig and Wigfield (2016), with cost treated as a separate category (Flake et al., 2015) and task value distinguished from interest and intrinsic motivation.
text.formatted: The classification was informed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Rosenzweig and Wigfield (2016)</ref>, with cost treated as a separate category <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Flake et al., 2015)</ref> and task value distinguished from interest and intrinsic motivation.

text.text: Mindset, attributions, and achievement goals were also retained as separate categories because their measures ask about different beliefs.
These groupings serve an analytical purpose rather than implying theoretical equivalence among the constructs within each category.
Competence refers to students' perceptions and experiences of their capability to succeed (Marsh et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Competence refers to students' perceptions and experiences of their capability to succeed <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Marsh et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In this meta-analysis, this construct serves as an umbrella category encompassing both competence-related beliefs (e.g., self-efficacy, self-concept, and expectancy beliefs) and perceived competence.

Self-efficacy refers to beliefs about one's capability to organize and execute the courses of action required to produce given attainments and is task-and context-specific rather than global (Bandura, 1977). Bandura (1997) identified four principal sources of self-efficacy: mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and physiological and affective states.
text.formatted: Self-efficacy refers to beliefs about one's capability to organize and execute the courses of action required to produce given attainments and is task-and context-specific rather than global <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bandura, 1977)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bandura (1997)</ref> identified four principal sources of self-efficacy: mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and physiological and affective states.

text.text: Academic self-concept, originating in the Shavelson model, represents broader evaluations of one's competence within an academic domain, shaped in part through social comparison (Marsh, 2007; Shavelson et al., 1976).
text.formatted: Academic self-concept, originating in the Shavelson model, represents broader evaluations of one's competence within an academic domain, shaped in part through social comparison <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Marsh, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Shavelson et al., 1976)</ref>.

text.text: Expectancy beliefs, a core construct of the SEVT framework, capture students' expectations about future performance in a course or subject (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: Expectancy beliefs, a core construct of the SEVT framework, capture students' expectations about future performance in a course or subject <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Within SDT, perceived competence reflects an individual's sense of effectiveness and capability during interactions with the environment (Ryan & Deci, 2017).
text.formatted: Within SDT, perceived competence reflects an individual's sense of effectiveness and capability during interactions with the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">(Ryan & Deci, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These constructs are theoretically distinguishable.

Self-efficacy concerns capability for specific tasks and is oriented toward future performance, whereas academic self-concept is a broader evaluation of competence within a domain, more anchored in past performance and shaped more strongly by social comparison; both draw on prior achievement experiences, and they show different antecedents and patterns of prediction (Bong & Skaalvik, 2003; Marsh et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Self-efficacy concerns capability for specific tasks and is oriented toward future performance, whereas academic self-concept is a broader evaluation of competence within a domain, more anchored in past performance and shaped more strongly by social comparison; both draw on prior achievement experiences, and they show different antecedents and patterns of prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Bong & Skaalvik, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Marsh et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Expectancy beliefs and perceived competence are likewise separable.
They are nevertheless aggregated here for the reasons given above; the grouping reflects the state of the literature rather than a claim of theoretical equivalence.

Psychosocial interventions target competence beliefs primarily by reframing the meaning of difficulty, encouraging students to construe struggle as a normal feature of learning rather than as evidence of insufficient ability.

Interest is an affective and cognitive attraction to a task (Hidi & Renninger, 2006), and intrinsic motivation, in SDT the most autonomous form of regulation, is engagement in an activity for its own sake (Ryan & Deci, 2002 , 2017).
text.formatted: Interest is an affective and cognitive attraction to a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Hidi & Renninger, 2006)</ref>, and intrinsic motivation, in SDT the most autonomous form of regulation, is engagement in an activity for its own sake <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">(Ryan & Deci, 2002</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: SEVT conceptualizes both as intrinsic value, the inherent interest or enjoyment of engaging in a task (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020 , 2024), so intrinsic value is grouped here with interest and intrinsic motivation rather than with utility or attainment value.
text.formatted: SEVT conceptualizes both as intrinsic value, the inherent interest or enjoyment of engaging in a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>, so intrinsic value is grouped here with interest and intrinsic motivation rather than with utility or attainment value.

text.text: Interventions rarely target intrinsic value directly; where interest increases, it is more commonly an indirect consequence of interventions that alter perceived relevance or reduce evaluative threat.

Task value refers to the perceived importance or usefulness of a task (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020 , 2024); students continuously evaluate how worthwhile a domain such as STEM is in relation to their goals, identities and aspirations, and these evaluations guide whether they engage, persist or withdraw (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024).
text.formatted: Task value refers to the perceived importance or usefulness of a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>; students continuously evaluate how worthwhile a domain such as STEM is in relation to their goals, identities and aspirations, and these evaluations guide whether they engage, persist or withdraw <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: SEVT distinguishes utility value, the usefulness of a task for current or future goals, from attainment value, the personal importance of doing well and its link to identity (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020 , 2024).
text.formatted: SEVT distinguishes utility value, the usefulness of a task for current or future goals, from attainment value, the personal importance of doing well and its link to identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The two are closely aligned in educational contexts and often measured together, so the present review combines them into a single task value category.
Like other value beliefs, task value is shaped by socializers such as parents, teachers and peers and by cultural norms and stereotypes (Kirkham et al., 2023; Murphy et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Like other value beliefs, task value is shaped by socializers such as parents, teachers and peers and by cultural norms and stereotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Kirkham et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Murphy et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Psychosocial interventions target task value most directly of any construct considered here, typically by prompting students to generate connections between course content and their own goals, interests or daily lives, on the premise that self-generated connections are more persuasive than those supplied by others.

Cost refers to the perceived negative aspects of engaging in a task, such as the effort required, the loss of valued alternatives and negative emotional experiences (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020; Flake et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Cost refers to the perceived negative aspects of engaging in a task, such as the effort required, the loss of valued alternatives and negative emotional experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Flake et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It counterbalances value, so a student may judge chemistry too costly if it demands substantial time, displaces other activities and risks emotional upset from failure.

Interventions addressing cost typically seek to reduce its perceived magnitude rather than its objective basis, for example by normalizing the effort a subject requires or by reframing the emotional experience of difficulty, and are correspondingly less able to affect costs grounded in students' material circumstances.
Achievement goals are the purposes students adopt in achievement settings and the standards by which they judge their progress (Elliot, 2023; Elliot & Sommet, 2023).
text.formatted: Achievement goals are the purposes students adopt in achievement settings and the standards by which they judge their progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Elliot, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Elliot & Sommet, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Achievement goal theory emerged from work distinguishing goals oriented toward developing competence from those oriented toward demonstrating it (Dweck & Leggett, 1988; Nicholls, 1984) and now distinguishes mastery from performance goals and approach from avoidance forms, giving four types (Elliot & McGregor, 2001; Guo et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Achievement goal theory emerged from work distinguishing goals oriented toward developing competence from those oriented toward demonstrating it <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Dweck & Leggett, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Nicholls, 1984)</ref> and now distinguishes mastery from performance goals and approach from avoidance forms, giving four types <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Elliot & McGregor, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Guo et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As few included trials measured achievement goals, all goal orientations are analyzed as one category (see Table 1).
text.formatted: As few included trials measured achievement goals, all goal orientations are analyzed as one category (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Achievement goal theory is a distinct tradition from SEVT, since goal orientations concern the purposes students adopt in achievement settings rather than their expectancies or values.

Interventions targeting achievement goals typically seek to shift students toward mastery orientations by emphasizing personal improvement over social comparison, though goal orientations develop across extended periods of schooling and may be harder to change through brief intervention than more situational appraisals.
Mindset refers to beliefs about the malleability of ability, from growth (incremental) to fixed (entity) theories (Dweck, 2006).
text.formatted: Mindset refers to beliefs about the malleability of ability, from growth (incremental) to fixed (entity) theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Dweck, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: These implicit theories were first proposed to explain why students of equivalent ability respond differently to failure (Dweck & Leggett, 1988).
text.formatted: These implicit theories were first proposed to explain why students of equivalent ability respond differently to failure <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Dweck & Leggett, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Students with a growth mindset tend to treat difficulty as part of learning and persist, whereas those with a fixed mindset tend to interpret setbacks as evidence of low ability and disengage, a contrast that matters particularly in complex, iterative STEM tasks (Bostwick et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2021; Degol et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Students with a growth mindset tend to treat difficulty as part of learning and persist, whereas those with a fixed mindset tend to interpret setbacks as evidence of low ability and disengage, a contrast that matters particularly in complex, iterative STEM tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Bostwick et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Campbell et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Degol et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike expectancy beliefs, which concern anticipated success, mindset concerns whether ability can be developed.
Mindset was therefore analyzed as a separate outcome category in this meta-analysis.

Mindset interventions typically present students with information about the malleability of the brain and ability and ask them to articulate that idea in their own words, often through writing addressed to a future student.
Attributions are the causal explanations individuals give for their successes and failures (Weiner, 1985 (Weiner, , 2019)).
text.formatted: Attributions are the causal explanations individuals give for their successes and failures <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">(Weiner, 1985</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">(Weiner, , 2019))</ref>.

text.text: Failure may be attributed to low ability, insufficient effort, task difficulty or lack of help, with consequences for subsequent motivation (Weiner, 1985).
text.formatted: Failure may be attributed to low ability, insufficient effort, task difficulty or lack of help, with consequences for subsequent motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">(Weiner, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Psychosocial interventions often encourage students to attribute challenges to controllable, improvable causes rather than fixed ability (Yeager & Walton, 2011), which has supported persistence and achievement in STEM (Hecht et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Psychosocial interventions often encourage students to attribute challenges to controllable, improvable causes rather than fixed ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Yeager & Walton, 2011)</ref>, which has supported persistence and achievement in STEM <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Hecht et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Attributions were specified as a category a priori but were represented by very few samples (see Table 1).
text.formatted: Attributions were specified as a category a priori but were represented by very few samples (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The category estimate is reported descriptively but not substantively interpreted.

Despite comparable academic performance, girls and women tend to report lower competence beliefs and interest and higher perceived costs in STEM, particularly in computer science, physics and engineering (Cheryan et al., 2011 (Cheryan et al., , 2013 (Cheryan et al., , 2017;; Eccles & Wigfield, 2024; Guo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Despite comparable academic performance, girls and women tend to report lower competence beliefs and interest and higher perceived costs in STEM, particularly in computer science, physics and engineering <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Cheryan et al., 2011</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Cheryan et al., , 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Cheryan et al., , 2017;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Eccles & Wigfield, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Guo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These differences are shaped by the messages of key socializers such as parents and teachers and by cultural norms about STEM competence and careers.
For example, attributing girls' success to effort and boys' to ability can erode girls' competence beliefs over time (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020 , 2023 , 2024).
text.formatted: For example, attributing girls' success to effort and boys' to ability can erode girls' competence beliefs over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Psychosocial interventions target these motivational processes, so they may be positioned to address barriers more commonly experienced by girls and women (Harackiewicz et al., 2023), making the gender composition of a sample a theoretically meaningful moderator.
text.formatted: Psychosocial interventions target these motivational processes, so they may be positioned to address barriers more commonly experienced by girls and women <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Harackiewicz et al., 2023)</ref>, making the gender composition of a sample a theoretically meaningful moderator.

text.text: This moderator operates at the study level, indicating whether effects differ across samples with varying proportions of girls and women, not whether individual girls and women respond differently from boys and men, which the aggregated data cannot test.
We distinguish gender composition from racial and ethnic underrepresentation.
Underrepresentation refers to a group's representation in STEM relative to its representation in the broader population, rather than numerical minority status within a particular STEM field.

In this review, underrepresented racial and ethnic groups comprise students identified as Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, consistent with the categories used in United States STEM reporting.

Asian students were not included in this grouping because they are not underrepresented in STEM overall relative to population base rates, although representation varies across disciplines and subgroups.

Where the discussion concerns stereotyping, exclusion, or differential treatment rather than representation, we use the term racially marginalized, recognizing that underrepresentation and marginalization are related but distinct concepts.
Gender, racial and ethnic background, and socioeconomic circumstances do not necessarily operate independently.
Their intersections may shape students' STEM experiences in ways that cannot be understood by considering each characteristic separately (Crenshaw, 1991; Ong et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Their intersections may shape students' STEM experiences in ways that cannot be understood by considering each characteristic separately <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Crenshaw, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Ong et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Family income and racial and ethnic background may also be correlated, making it difficult to distinguish their respective contributions without considering them jointly.

Students from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups are often racially marginalized in STEM settings and encounter sociocultural barriers that shape their STEM motivation (Harackiewicz et al., 2023), and differences in their motivational beliefs reflect these experiences rather than differences in academic capability (Dotterer, 2022; Harackiewicz et al., 2016; Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009).
text.formatted: Students from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups are often racially marginalized in STEM settings and encounter sociocultural barriers that shape their STEM motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Harackiewicz et al., 2023)</ref>, and differences in their motivational beliefs reflect these experiences rather than differences in academic capability <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Dotterer, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Harackiewicz et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: In SEVT terms, such differences arise through socialization and context, including stereotypes, belonging uncertainty and evaluative climates, rather than from students themselves (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: In SEVT terms, such differences arise through socialization and context, including stereotypes, belonging uncertainty and evaluative climates, rather than from students themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions built on this account can narrow gaps.

In an introductory biology course, a utility-value intervention reduced the course-grade gap between students from underrepresented groups who were also the first in their families to attend college and continuing-generation majority students by 61% (Harackiewicz et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In an introductory biology course, a utility-value intervention reduced the course-grade gap between students from underrepresented groups who were also the first in their families to attend college and continuing-generation majority students by 61% <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Harackiewicz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Motivational disparities in STEM are not attributable solely to students' backgrounds.

Learning environments can also create and reinforce barriers through microaggressions, exclusionary practices, inequitable evaluation and discipline, and unequal access to mentoring and research opportunities (McGee, 2020; Ong et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Learning environments can also create and reinforce barriers through microaggressions, exclusionary practices, inequitable evaluation and discipline, and unequal access to mentoring and research opportunities <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">(McGee, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Ong et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Faculty beliefs that ability is fixed have also been associated with larger racial achievement gaps and lower student motivation (Canning et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Faculty beliefs that ability is fixed have also been associated with larger racial achievement gaps and lower student motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Canning et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These structural and institutional conditions are important when considering psychosocial interventions.
Helping students reinterpret academic difficulties does not, by itself, change the environments that produce or sustain those difficulties.

Racially marginalized students also face stereotypes and socialization messages that can undermine belonging and perceived competence (Dotterer, 2022; Totonchi et al., 2021; Totonchi, Francis, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Racially marginalized students also face stereotypes and socialization messages that can undermine belonging and perceived competence <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Dotterer, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Totonchi et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Totonchi, Francis, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In a four-year longitudinal study of students from groups underrepresented in STEM, for example, higher initial stereotype threat was associated with faster declines in attainment value and faster increases in perceived cost across college (Totonchi et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In a four-year longitudinal study of students from groups underrepresented in STEM, for example, higher initial stereotype threat was associated with faster declines in attainment value and faster increases in perceived cost across college <ref type="bibr">(Totonchi et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions that strengthen perceived relevance, clarify pathways to success and address belonging may therefore be particularly effective for students from groups underrepresented in STEM, which makes the racial and ethnic composition of samples a theoretically relevant moderator.
This is among the first meta-analyses to systematically synthesize evidence on psychosocial interventions targeting motivational processes specifically within STEM contexts.

Rather than focusing on instructional methods or pedagogical approaches, this review centers on motivation, namely, the internal processes that energize and direct students' engagement, persistence, and decision-making in STEM learning (Reeve, 2025).
text.formatted: Rather than focusing on instructional methods or pedagogical approaches, this review centers on motivation, namely, the internal processes that energize and direct students' engagement, persistence, and decision-making in STEM learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Reeve, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Guided by SEVT as the integrating framework, the research questions examine the overall effects of psychosocial interventions on STEM motivation, differences across intervention types and motivational outcomes, and variation associated with sample gender and racial/ethnic composition.
These analyses assess intervention effects and study-level variation rather than directly testing the psychological pathways proposed by SEVT.
The four research questions (RQ) are as follows.
RQ1.
Do psychosocial interventions overall improve students' motivation in STEM subjects?
RQ2.
Do the effects of psychosocial interventions on STEM motivation differ by intervention type (e.g., task value, framing, or personal values)?
RQ3.
Do the effects of psychosocial interventions on STEM motivation differ across motivational outcomes (e.g., task value, cost, competence, interest, goals, or mindset)?
RQ4.

Do the effects of psychosocial interventions on STEM motivation differ across samples of differing composition, specifically by the proportion of participants who are girls and women and by the proportion from groups underrepresented in STEM?

This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) (Page et al., 2021) and the Meta-Analysis Reporting Standards (Cooper, 2008).
text.formatted: This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Page et al., 2021)</ref> and the Meta-Analysis Reporting Standards <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Cooper, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The study protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF), and all metaanalytic data, coding materials, and analysis code are publicly available (see https://osf.io/zc9wg/overview?view_only=cee939c3d42c42b69dd2abff42092f48).
text.formatted: The study protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF), and all metaanalytic data, coding materials, and analysis code are publicly available (see <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/zc9wg/overview?view_only=cee939c3d42c42b69dd2abff42092f48">https://osf.io/zc9wg/overview?   view_only=cee939c3d42c42b69dd2abff42092f48</ref>).

text.text: Deviations from the preregistered protocol are documented in the OSF repository.
Research Question 5, on engagement outcomes, was removed before analysis to keep the focus on motivational constructs, and the construct categories were updated in line with current theory.

Two exploratory analyses were added after registration: the proportion of participants from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM as a sample-level moderator, and a comparison of EVT-and SEVT-framed samples (Supplemental Note S1).
All other procedures followed the preregistered plan.
Studies were required to meet inclusion criteria to be included in the meta-analysis.
Supplemental Table S2 details the criteria.
text.formatted: Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S2</ref> details the criteria.

text.text: For inclusion in the meta-analysis, the study needed to: (i) be quantitative in design; (ii) present original data; (iii) include students enrolled in primary, secondary, or tertiary education; (iv) assess at least one motivational construct related to STEM learning, identified using the broad definition of motivation as the internal processes that energize, direct and sustain goal-directed behavior (Reeve, 2025) Family income and socioeconomic indicators were extracted where available.
text.formatted: For inclusion in the meta-analysis, the study needed to: (i) be quantitative in design; (ii) present original data; (iii) include students enrolled in primary, secondary, or tertiary education; (iv) assess at least one motivational construct related to STEM learning, identified using the broad definition of motivation as the internal processes that energize, direct and sustain goal-directed behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Reeve, 2025)</ref> Family income and socioeconomic indicators were extracted where available.

text.text: However, no included study reported family income directly, and other socioeconomic indicators, such as financial aid and parental education, were reported inconsistently.
Consequently, socioeconomic background could not be examined as a moderator.
The following databases were first searched for articles in July 2024 meeting the eligibility criteria: Scopus (Elsevier), PsycINFO, Education Source, ERIC (EBSCO), and Web of Science.
Several pilot searches were conducted with a variety of search term configurations.
These database searches found 12,092 candidate studies.

We searched titles and abstracts in the five databases with terms for five concept blocks: interventions, STEM domains, educational settings and populations, randomized or experimental designs, and motivational outcomes (for example, utility value, self-efficacy, mindset, perceived cost and achievement goals).
The full database-specific search strings are provided in Supplemental Table S3.
text.formatted: The full database-specific search strings are provided in Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>.

text.text: The initial database search was conducted in July 2024, followed by backward and forward citation searching in October 2024.
The searches were updated in August 2026 using the same search terms and eligibility criteria.
Two researchers independently screened records at the title and abstract stage (κ = .89) and at full text (κ = .92), with disagreements resolved through discussion.
Following final verification, 52 independent samples from 50 papers were included, contributing 348 effect sizes.
Figure 1 presents the screening and verification process, and Supplemental Table S4 lists the 52 included samples.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> presents the screening and verification process, and Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S4</ref> lists the 52 included samples.

text.text: Data were extracted into an Excel coding sheet, which was piloted on three included studies.

Extracted data included study characteristics (e.g., year of publication), sample characteristics (e.g., age and gender composition), intervention characteristics (e.g., task value, framing or personal values), motivation constructs, and effect sizes.

Extraction was carried out independently and in duplicate by two reviewers, and the two sets of codings were then compared for consistency and accuracy (κ = .88); conflicts were resolved through discussion between the reviewers and, where necessary, with other members of the team.

All coded values were then verified against the source reports, and against author-provided raw data where available; this verification identified and corrected several transcription errors, the most consequential being a study in which standard errors had been recorded in place of standard deviations.

Motivational constructs were categorized into the seven categories described above; the attributions category rests on only three effect sizes and, although carried into the construct moderator, is described narratively rather than interpreted (see Supplemental Table S1 for the full list of psychological constructs within each category).
text.formatted: Motivational constructs were categorized into the seven categories described above; the attributions category rests on only three effect sizes and, although carried into the construct moderator, is described narratively rather than interpreted (see Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> for the full list of psychological constructs within each category).

text.text: Participant gender composition was extracted as reported in the original studies.

Most included studies used binary categories without specifying whether sex or gender identity was assessed, so the moderator was operationalized as the proportion of participants reported as girls and women.
Nonbinary participants, where reported, were too few to form a separate category.

The proportion of participants from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM was coded as a sample-level moderator, comprising students identified as Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander.

Students in all other groups, including Asian and White students, formed the remaining share; Asian students were not counted as underrepresented, consistent with the definition given in the Introduction, but were not reclassified as White.
This moderator was not specified in advance and was examined as an exploratory sample-level moderator.

This measure represents sample composition rather than individual experiences of marginalization or differential treatment, and it cannot show whether intervention effects differ between individual students from underrepresented and other groups.
An underrepresented proportion could be derived for 29 of the 33 samples that reported racial and ethnic composition.
Where studies reported Hispanic or Latino identification separately from race, each participant was counted once, using non-Hispanic racial categories alongside the Hispanic or Latino percentage.

Interventions were coded into the three families described above, following Harackiewicz and Priniski (2018), on the basis of the component the trial manipulated rather than the outcomes it measured: task value interventions, in which students generated or received connections between course content and their own goals, interests or daily lives (e.g., utility-value writing, personal relevance reflections); framing interventions, which addressed how students interpret difficulty, ability and progress (e.g., growth-mindset messages, struggle reframing, attributional strategies); and personal values interventions, which addressed identity, self-worth and belonging (e.g., values affirmation, role models, belonging interventions).

A trial was coded as Combined only when it identified the components it brought together, in its arm labels or its description of the intervention; a single program whose sessions happened to touch on several families was coded to the family of its manipulated component (Supplemental Table S5 lists the components each Combined trial names).

text.text: The category draws on four independent samples and is defined by a declared combination of components rather than a shared active ingredient, so its estimate is not interpreted as the effect of a distinct approach.
Motivational outcomes were coded into the seven categories described in Targeted Motivational Constructs.
All seven entered the construct moderator analysis.
Attributions, represented by only three effect sizes from three samples, was discussed narratively rather than interpreted as a substantive category estimate.

Categories were operationalized as set out below, Supplemental Table S1 lists the construct labels coded within each category, and the construct coding of every effect size is provided with the data on OSF.
text.formatted: Categories were operationalized as set out below, Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> lists the construct labels coded within each category, and the construct coding of every effect size is provided with the data on OSF.

text.text: Competence comprised measures of self-efficacy, academic self-concept, expectancy beliefs and perceived competence, all of which index students' perceptions of their capability to succeed.
Measures of achievement and of general self-esteem were not coded within this category; students' self-assessed ability in a subject was coded here as a perception of capability.
Interest and intrinsic motivation comprised measures of individual interest, situational interest, and intrinsic motivation, each indexing enjoyment of or attraction to the activity itself.

Measures of enjoyment reported as an outcome of performance rather than of the activity itself were not coded here, nor were measures of engagement or participation, which index behavior rather than the motivational state underlying it.

Task value comprised measures of the utility and attainment components of subjective task value such as perceived usefulness of a subject for daily life, schooling or future career, and perceived personal importance of succeeding in it.
Intrinsic value was coded within the interest category, and cost was coded as a separate category.
Measures of general attitudes toward a subject were coded here where items referenced usefulness or importance and excluded otherwise.

Cost comprised measures of perceived cost across the facets identified by Flake et al. (2015), effort required, opportunity cost, and emotional or psychological cost, together with composite measures that did not distinguish these facets.
text.formatted: Cost comprised measures of perceived cost across the facets identified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Flake et al. (2015)</ref>, effort required, opportunity cost, and emotional or psychological cost, together with composite measures that did not distinguish these facets.

text.text: Anxiety tied to the subject or its assessment, such as mathematics or test anxiety, was coded as emotional cost; measures of workload or time demands reported as objective features of a course rather than as student perceptions were not coded here.
Cost effect sizes were reverse-coded so that positive values indicate lower perceived cost.
Goals comprised measures of achievement goal orientation, including mastery and performance orientations in both approach and avoidance forms.

Goal outcomes were coded at the level of the reported subscale, including mastery-approach, performance-approach, performance-avoidance, and intrinsic goal orientation from the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (treated as a mastery-related indicator).
Performance-avoidance outcomes were reverse-coded so that positive effects indicated reductions in avoidance orientation.
Only six samples measured goals, and four of these distinguished mastery from performance orientations, so these outcomes were analyzed together as a single category.
Measures of goal setting, goal commitment and future-oriented self-representations were not coded within this category.
Mindset comprised measures of implicit theories of ability, including both incremental and entity formulations and both domain-general and STEM-specific measures.
Where entity-theory items were reported, effect sizes were reverse-coded so that positive values indicate movement toward an incremental view.
Measures of causal attributions for success or failure were coded separately.

Effect sizes were reconstructed from arm-level descriptive statistics wherever available, so that each sampling variance is an independent-participants quantity by construction and does not inherit any clustering adjustment made in the source study's own analysis.

Four sources of statistical dependency were therefore addressed in sequence, each at the stage at which it arises: clustered allocation, shared comparison groups in multi-arm trials, multiple outcomes measured on the same participants, and repeated measurement of the same outcome.

For the 17 cluster-randomized samples (134 effect sizes), sampling variances were inflated by a design effect, DE = 1 + (m X -1) × ICC, where m X is the mean cluster size; the effect sizes themselves were left unchanged (Higgins et al., 2019, section 23.1.5).
text.formatted: For the 17 cluster-randomized samples (134 effect sizes), sampling variances were inflated by a design effect, DE = 1 + (m X -1) × ICC, where m X is the mean cluster size; the effect sizes themselves were left unchanged <ref type="bibr">(Higgins et al., 2019, section 23.1.5)</ref>.

text.text: Intraclass correlations were taken from the primary reports where available, computed from the authors' archived data for one trial, and otherwise taken from a closely related trial or the median of the reported values (trial-level values .010 to .118, Mdn = .050), giving design effects of 1.22 to 4.53 (Mdn = 1.93).
The source of every intraclass correlation is given in Supplemental Table S6.
