text.text: The remaining dependencies were captured in a single working variance-covariance matrix built with the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010).
text.formatted: The remaining dependencies were captured in a single working variance-covariance matrix built with the metafor package <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">(Viechtbauer, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: These were effect sizes sharing a comparison group (200 effect sizes in 14 samples), multiple outcomes measured on the same participants (an assumed correlation of .70 within a construct category and .50 across categories), and repeated measurements of the same outcome (an autocorrelation of .70 between adjacent occasions; 12 samples).
The matrix was supplied to a three-level random-effects model, with effect sizes nested within samples, estimated by restricted maximum likelihood.
Moderators were tested with omnibus F tests.
Heterogeneity is reported as Q, as the variance components τ² ₂ and τ² ₃ , which estimate the ₍ ₎ ₍ ₎ absolute magnitude of variance in true effects within and between samples, and as I².

Two decompositions of I² are given because they answer different questions: the share of total variance, including sampling error, attributable to heterogeneity at each level, following Cheung (2014); and the share of the heterogeneity itself lying between as against within samples.
text.formatted: Two decompositions of I² are given because they answer different questions: the share of total variance, including sampling error, attributable to heterogeneity at each level, following <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Cheung (2014)</ref>; and the share of the heterogeneity itself lying between as against within samples.

text.text: A 95% prediction interval is reported for the effect expected in a new trial.

Moderators were examined by coding effect sizes into mutually exclusive categories such as intervention type used in the study, motivational processes measured as an outcome of the intervention, and student characteristics (sample gender composition, coded as the proportion of girls and women, and the proportion of participants from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM, which was available only for studies conducted in the United States).

Additional robustness moderators were examined including age, subject domain, intervention format, duration of intervention, application frequency, education setting and country as well as risk of bias.

Effect sizes are interpreted against the effects observed in comparable syntheses rather than against fixed benchmarks, because benchmarks derived for achievement outcomes (Kraft, 2020) do not transfer to self-reported motivational beliefs.

text.text: Overall, 348 effect sizes were extracted from 52 independent samples reported in 50 papers.
Every extracted effect size could be expressed on a common metric and all 348 entered the final model.
The dependency structure modeled directly accommodates the repeated measurements, shared comparison groups and multiple outcomes per sample, so no effect size was excluded on these grounds.

Where means and standard deviations were available (329 effect sizes), Hedges' g was calculated directly using the standardized mean difference with a small-sample bias correction (Hedges & Olkin, 1985).

text.text: The Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB2) was used to assess the risk of bias for each study across five domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of the outcome, and bias in selection of the reported result (Sterne et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB2) was used to assess the risk of bias for each study across five domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of the outcome, and bias in selection of the reported result <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">(Sterne et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Of the final set, 35 samples were assessed using the individually randomized version of RoB2 and 17 using the cluster-randomized variant, where randomization occurred at the class, school, or teacher level.

Within these domains, key indicators included whether randomization was adequately concealed, whether manipulation checks were reported to verify intervention delivery, whether outcome measures demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity, and the degree of attrition or missing data at follow-up.

Motivational outcomes in this literature are almost invariably self-reported; blinding of outcome assessment is therefore not achievable, and measurement of the outcome is accordingly one of the two domains on which the fewest studies were rated at low risk (14 of 52, alongside selection of the reported result at 15 of 52).
This follows from a feature of the evaluation tradition rather than from the conduct of individual trials.
Quality assessment was conducted independently and in duplicate by two reviewers (κ = .87), with conflicts resolved by a third team member.
Overall risk-of-bias judgments were derived from the domain-level assessments using the standard RoB2 criteria.

A study was rated at high risk when at least one domain was rated high, at some concerns when at least one domain raised some concerns and none was rated high, and at low risk when all domains were rated low.

RoB2 also allows a study with some concerns in several domains to be rated high overall, so the two raters reviewed the 14 samples with some concerns in two or more domains; none was judged to warrant a high-risk rating.
Publication bias and small-study effects were examined using several complementary approaches.
First, publication type was tested as a categorical moderator to determine whether effect sizes differed between samples reported in peer-reviewed sources and those that were not.
Publication year was also tested as a continuous moderator to examine possible time-lag or dissemination patterns.
Second, a contourenhanced funnel plot was inspected for visual evidence of asymmetry.

Third, a multilevel Egger regression was estimated within the same three-level framework and with the same working covariance matrix, entering the square root of the sampling variance of the effect size as a predictor and treating the significance of that slope as the test of funnel asymmetry or small-study effects (Egger et al., 1997; Pustejovsky & Rodgers, 2019; Rodgers & Pustejovsky, 2021).
text.formatted: Third, a multilevel Egger regression was estimated within the same three-level framework and with the same working covariance matrix, entering the square root of the sampling variance of the effect size as a predictor and treating the significance of that slope as the test of funnel asymmetry or small-study effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Egger et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Pustejovsky & Rodgers, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Rodgers & Pustejovsky, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The Egger slope is a function of the sampling variances, and those variances depend in turn on the intraclass, concurrent-outcome and longitudinal correlations assumed in the working matrix.
The test was therefore also repeated under the dispersion adjustment described below.

Fourth, publication bias was examined using a multilevel robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA; Bartoš et al., 2023; Maier et al., 2023), which averages across models with and without an intervention effect, heterogeneity and publication selection; the selection component comprised six weight-function models, with effect sizes clustered within samples.
text.formatted: Fourth, publication bias was examined using a multilevel robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Bartoš et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Maier et al., 2023)</ref>, which averages across models with and without an intervention effect, heterogeneity and publication selection; the selection component comprised six weight-function models, with effect sizes clustered within samples.

text.text: The pooled and moderator estimates rest on correlations in the working matrix that are partly assumed, and on model-based standard errors, which can be too small when heterogeneity is high and the number of samples is modest.
We therefore checked them in two ways.

First, the matrix was rebuilt and the pooled estimate and the significant moderators refitted across 44 combinations of these correlations: the within-category correlation varied from .5 to .9, the between-category correlation from .3 to .7, the autocorrelation across .5, .7 and .9, and the intraclass correlation from .02 to .15.

Second, the pooled estimate and the main moderator tests were repeated with a Knapp-Hartung-type dispersion adjustment, which widens the standard errors whenever the effect sizes vary more than the model expects.
The standard Knapp-Hartung adjustment is not available for three-level models, so its multivariate analogue was used and is reported as a sensitivity analysis.

The model was also refitted by omitting one sample at a time, to check whether any single sample drove the pooled estimate, and separately excluding the samples rated at high risk of bias and the cluster-randomized samples.
In the final analysis, data were synthesized from 348 effect sizes drawn from 52 independent samples, reported in 50 papers.
Every extracted effect size could be placed on a common metric and entered the model.

Thirty-five samples were randomized at the level of the individual and 17 at the level of the cluster (13 by class, three by school and one by teacher); the cluster-randomized samples contribute 134 effect sizes.
Fourteen samples contributed more than one intervention arm against a shared comparison group, and 12 measured at more than one occasion.
The mean participant age was 17.73 years (SD = 4.43, reported by 35 of the 52 samples).
Most samples were drawn from the United States (n = 37); the remaining 15 came from eight other countries, most often Germany and South Korea (four each; Supplemental Table S8).
text.formatted: Most samples were drawn from the United States (n = 37); the remaining 15 came from eight other countries, most often Germany and South Korea (four each; Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>).

text.text: The included samples were reported in publications from 2009 to 2026 (median 2023).
One sample was published before 2010, 15 between 2010 and 2019, and 36 from 2020 onward.

As illustrated graphically in Figure 2 and as reported statistically in the upper part of Table 1, the three-level random-effects model with the full working covariance matrix identified a positive overall effect of psychosocial interventions on motivation outcomes, g = 0.12, 95% CI [0.06, 0.17], SE = 0.03, t(51) = 4.38, p < .001.

text.text: The variance components were τ² ₂ = .003 within samples and τ² ₃ = .023 between them, so that 88.7% of ₍ ₎ ₍ ₎ the heterogeneity lies between samples and 11.3% within them.

Expressed instead as shares of total variance including sampling error (Cheung, 2014), heterogeneity accounts for 65.7% of the total variance, with 58.3 percentage points between samples and 7.4 within them.

text.text: On either decomposition heterogeneity is concentrated between samples rather than among the effect sizes a single sample contributes.
Modeling the dependency among effect sizes raised the total sampling variance from 10.67 to 11.88, correcting the overstated precision of effect sizes from cluster-randomized and multi-arm trials.
The 95% prediction interval for the effect in a new study was [-0.21, 0.45].

The positive and reliably estimated average effect provides evidence that psychosocial interventions can improve STEM motivation, while the prediction interval indicates that effects may vary considerably across settings, with some experiencing larger benefits and others showing limited or no improvement.
The pooled estimate should therefore be interpreted as an average across a heterogeneous literature rather than as the expected effect in any particular classroom.
The magnitude of this estimate is interpreted against comparable syntheses.

Meta-analyses of mindset interventions evaluated against academic achievement report effects of d = 0.08 (Sisk et al., 2018) and d = 0.05, falling to d = 0.02 among studies meeting the highest evidentiary standards (Macnamara & Burgoyne, 2023), whereas the corresponding estimate here, for mindset measured as a motivational belief, is g = 0.16.

text.text: Effects on self-reported beliefs would be expected to exceed effects on achievement, as these outcomes are more proximal to intervention content, so the pooled estimate of g = 0.12 is small even on the outcomes where these interventions should register most strongly.

Intervention types were grouped into four categories: Task Value, Framing, Personal Values, and a Combined category for trials that identify two or more components delivered together (see Supplemental Table S5 for the individual interventions coded within each category).

text.text: Intervention type did not moderate intervention effectiveness, F(3, 344) = 0.06, p = .981.

The four categories yielded closely comparable estimates: Personal Values g = 0.14, 95% CI [0.01, 0.27], p = .039, 52 effect sizes from seven samples; Task The confidence intervals around all four categories overlap substantially, and neither the omnibus test nor the individual estimates support the conclusion that these categories differ from one another.

Motivational construct moderated intervention effectiveness, F(6, 341) = 5.84, p < .001 (Figure 3), and it is the only moderator that explains appreciable variance among the effect sizes a single sample contributes (R² ₂ = 33.1%, R² ₃ = 6.4%), as would be expected of an outcome-level characteristic.

text.text: The ₍ ₎ ₍ ₎ largest estimates were for task value (g = 0.18, 95% CI [0.12, 0.23], p < .001; 93 effect sizes from 32 samples) and mindset (g = 0.16, 95% CI [0.06, 0.25], p = .001; 11 effect sizes from six samples), followed by interest (g = 0.10, 95% CI [0.04, 0.16], p < .001; 76 effect sizes from 33 samples) and competence (g = 0.09, 95% CI [0.03, 0.15], p = .004; 76 effect sizes from 28 samples), each with a confidence interval excluding zero; goals (g = 0.09, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.21], p = .163; 42 effect sizes from six samples) and cost (g = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.10], p = .248; 47 effect sizes from 15 samples) were not distinguishable from zero (Table 1).

text.text: The sparse attributions category (g = 0.19, three effect sizes from three samples) is reported for completeness and is not interpreted.
The mindset and goals estimates, each from six samples, are provisional.
Forty of the 52 samples measured more than one category, in differing combinations, so differences between categories partly reflect differences between the samples in which each was assessed.
Sample gender composition was not associated with intervention effectiveness, F(1, 49) = 0.09, p = .760, across 344 effect sizes from 51 samples.

The moderator was coded as the proportion of participants reported as girls and women (range 0-1), so the slope represents the predicted difference in g across the full range of sample composition (b = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.28, 0.38]).
The moderator accounted for none of the variance at either level.
The estimate is a null centered almost exactly on zero, although the interval remains wide enough that a small association in either direction cannot be excluded.

It represents a sample-level association between composition and intervention effectiveness and should not be interpreted as evidence about individual-level gender differences in intervention effects (see Figure 4).
text.formatted: It represents a sample-level association between composition and intervention effectiveness and should not be interpreted as evidence about individual-level gender differences in intervention effects (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: The proportion of participants from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM was examined as a sample-level moderator across 29 samples (205 effect sizes).
Of the 52 included samples, 19 did not report racial or ethnic composition and four reported it too coarsely for this analysis (for example, only White and non-White participants).
The proportion of underrepresented students was not significantly associated with intervention effects, b = 0.26, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.63], F(1, 27) = 2.16, p = .153.

An exploratory contrast between majority-URM and other samples was significant at a 50% threshold (difference = 0.24, 95% CI [0.04, 0.45], p = .022) but not at 40% or 60% (p = .110 and .291), or after excluding Falco and Summers (2019) or Im (2013) (p = .102 and .078).
text.formatted: An exploratory contrast between majority-URM and other samples was significant at a 50% threshold (difference = 0.24, 95% CI [0.04, 0.45], p = .022) but not at 40% or 60% (p = .110 and .291), or after excluding <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Falco and Summers (2019)</ref> or Im (2013) (p = .102 and .078).

text.text: Given this sensitivity and the absence of a significant continuous association, the categorical result was not interpreted further.

All 33 samples reporting racial or ethnic composition were conducted in the United States, of which 29 provided sufficient information to calculate the proportion of participants from groups underrepresented in STEM.
The restriction of this moderator analysis to U.S. samples therefore reflects the available evidence rather than an assumption that racial and ethnic data are not collected in other countries.

To examine the robustness of intervention effects across contextual and methodological factors, seven additional moderators were tested: age, subject domain, intervention format, education setting, country, application frequency and duration of intervention.

Age, subject domain, education setting and country did not moderate intervention effects (age: F(1, 33) = 0.42, p = .524, across 243 effect sizes from the 35 samples reporting mean age; subject domain: F(3, 48) = 0.43, p = .733; education setting: F(2, 49) = 1.50, p = .233; country: F(3, 48) = 0.88, p = .461).

Intervention format moderated effects in the primary model, F(2, 345) = 3.55, p = .030, with mixed delivery yielding the largest estimate (g = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.53]) ahead of in-person (g = 0.17, 95% CI [0.09, 0.24]) and online delivery (g = 0.07, 95% CI [0.003, 0.14]), and the moderator accounted for 17.4% of between-sample variance.

Format does not survive the dispersion adjustment reported below (p = .057), and the mixed-delivery estimate rests on 12 effect sizes from three samples and is confounded with education setting and with intervention type, so it is reported as provisional.
The non-significant moderator results should not be interpreted as evidence of consistent effects across contexts.
Given the heterogeneity of motivational outcomes and the limited number of samples within some moderator categories, these analyses may have limited sensitivity to detect contextual differences.

Application frequency did not moderate effects (F(1, 339) = 0.23, p = .629), while duration of intervention did (F(1, 205) = 5.75, p = .017, R² ₃ = 13.0%), with each additional hour of intervention associated with an ₍ ₎ increase of g = 0.07, 95% CI [0.01, 0.12].

This estimate rests on the 207 effect sizes from 32 samples that reported intervention duration in a form permitting extraction, and it only narrowly survives the dispersion adjustment reported below (p = .047).

Risk of bias, assessed using the Cochrane RoB2 tool and entered as the overall RoB2 judgment, did not significantly moderate intervention effects (F(2, 49) = 1.52, p = .228); this result is reported in full under Sensitivity Analysis below.

An exploratory comparison of EVT-and SEVT-framed samples published from 2020 onward yielded a nominally significant difference (p = .045) that was not robust to sensitivity analyses (Supplemental Note S1).

text.text: Publication bias and small-study effects were examined using several complementary approaches.

Publication type did not moderate effect sizes, F(1, 50) = 0.40, p = .530, indicating that effects did not differ systematically between the 46 samples reported in peer-reviewed sources (g = 0.11) and the six that were not (g = 0.18), the latter comprising dissertations and other unrefereed reports.
Publication year also did not moderate effect sizes, F(1, 50) = 0.62, p = .433, suggesting no clear evidence of time-lag or disseminationrelated patterns.
Visual inspection of the funnel plot indicated effect sizes broadly distributed around the pooled estimate, with greater dispersion among the less precise samples (see Figure 5).
text.formatted: Visual inspection of the funnel plot indicated effect sizes broadly distributed around the pooled estimate, with greater dispersion among the less precise samples (see Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>).

text.text: The multilevel Egger regression yielded a positive but non-significant slope, b = 0.67, 95% CI [-0.01, 1.36], F(1, 346) = 3.71, p = .055 (p = .083 under the Knapp-Hartung-type dispersion adjustment), indicating that small-study effects cannot be ruled out.
In contrast, Bayesian selection models provided strong evidence favoring the absence of p-value-based publication selection (inclusion BF = 0.035), with estimated selection weights close to 1.
The model-averaged, selection-adjusted effect was g = 0.13, 95% CrI [0.04, 0.21], slightly larger than the primary estimate (g = 0.12).
These findings support the robustness of the pooled effect to the publicationselection mechanisms examined.
The robustness of the pooled estimate was examined across 44 specifications of the working covariance matrix, each rebuilt from scratch and refitted.
The pooled estimate lay between g = 0.11 and g = 0.13 in every one, against a primary estimate of g = 0.12, and the confidence interval excluded zero in all 44.

Varying the intraclass correlation between .02 and .15 moved the pooled estimate from g = 0.13 to g = 0.12, and varying the within-category correlation, the between-category correlation and the longitudinal autocorrelation across the remaining 39 specifications moved it between g = 0.11 and g = 0.12.

Under the Knapp-Hartung-type dispersion adjustment, the standard error of the pooled estimate increased by 10.9%, widening the interval from [0.06, 0.17] to [0.06, 0.18]; the pooled effect remains significant.

Moderation by motivational construct is robust; it is significant at every setting of the intraclass, concurrent-outcome and longitudinal correlations (p ≤ .020) and under the dispersion adjustment (p < .001).

Risk of bias (p = .228) and small-study bias (p = .055) are not significant in the primary specification and remain non-significant under the dispersion adjustment (p = .299 and p = .083).
The pooled effect itself is unaffected by any of these choices.

Refits excluding samples at high risk of bias are reported below.
Risk of bias, entered as a categorical moderator using the overall RoB2 judgments, did not significantly moderate intervention effects, F(2, 49) = 1.52, p = .228.
Excluding the 32 samples rated at high risk yielded a positive pooled effect, g = 0.10, 95% CI [0.01, 0.18], p = .035, across the remaining 20 samples (166 effect sizes).

text.text: This meta-analysis examined whether psychosocial interventions improve students' motivation in STEM and whether their effects differ across intervention types, motivational outcomes, and sample composition, drawing on randomized controlled trials.
Throughout this discussion, we distinguish findings from the meta-analysis, observations from individual included trials, and theoretical interpretations informed by the broader literature.

Individual trials are used to illustrate the intervention approaches and contexts represented in the synthesis, while theoretical explanations are presented as possibilities rather than findings established by the meta-analysis.
Intervention effects varied significantly across motivational outcome categories.

Among the six categories with enough samples to interpret, the largest estimated effects were observed for task value and mindset, followed by interest and competence, whereas effects on perceived cost and achievement goals were not statistically distinguishable from zero.

Interventions raised task value (g = 0.18) across 32 samples, the largest estimate among the principal outcomes and one of the most studied. Curry et al. (2020) reported larger effects when students generated personal connections to learning material than when its relevance was communicated directly.
text.formatted: Interventions raised task value (g = 0.18) across 32 samples, the largest estimate among the principal outcomes and one of the most studied. <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Curry et al. (2020)</ref> reported larger effects when students generated personal connections to learning material than when its relevance was communicated directly.

text.text: This finding is consistent with accounts in which generating relevance connections for oneself is key to how these interventions raise task value (Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009), and with laboratory experiments comparing self-generated and directly communicated utility-value information (Canning & Harackiewicz, 2015).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with accounts in which generating relevance connections for oneself is key to how these interventions raise task value <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009)</ref>, and with laboratory experiments comparing self-generated and directly communicated utility-value information <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Canning & Harackiewicz, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The present meta-analysis did not test this comparison.

Interventions raised mindset beliefs (g = 0.16), the second-largest estimate, though on the smallest evidence base of the well-populated categories (11 effect sizes from six samples), so the estimate is provisional.
Among the contributing trials, Burnette et al. (2020) reported that beliefs about ability moved together with the perceived worth of STEM.
text.formatted: Among the contributing trials, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Burnette et al. (2020)</ref> reported that beliefs about ability moved together with the perceived worth of STEM.

text.text: Research beyond the present sample proposes that viewing ability as developable reduces the threat associated with difficulty (Dweck, 2006; Yeager & Dweck, 2012); the present evidence is consistent with this account but too limited to test it.
text.formatted: Research beyond the present sample proposes that viewing ability as developable reduces the threat associated with difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Dweck, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">Yeager & Dweck, 2012)</ref>; the present evidence is consistent with this account but too limited to test it.

text.text: Interest outcomes yielded smaller but reliably positive effects across 33 samples (g = 0.10), so on average the interventions raised interest, although only six samples individually showed gains with confidence intervals excluding zero.

Five of these were utility-value interventions that asked students to connect science or mathematics to their own lives, the largest in two primary science programs in South Korea delivered within regular lessons over several sessions (S. H. Park et al., 2026; Shin et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Five of these were utility-value interventions that asked students to connect science or mathematics to their own lives, the largest in two primary science programs in South Korea delivered within regular lessons over several sessions (S. H. <ref type="bibr">Park et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Shin et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The sixth was a growth-mindset program for university computer science students (Burnette et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The sixth was a growth-mindset program for university computer science students <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Burnette et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Research beyond the present sample suggests why the average gain was smaller than for task value.

Interest develops gradually through sustained engagement, whereas task value can shift quickly when students are helped to see the relevance of what they are learning (Hidi & Renninger, 2026; Hulleman et al., 2010), so brief interventions may trigger situational interest without it consolidating into individual interest.
text.formatted: Interest develops gradually through sustained engagement, whereas task value can shift quickly when students are helped to see the relevance of what they are learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Hidi & Renninger, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Hulleman et al., 2010)</ref>, so brief interventions may trigger situational interest without it consolidating into individual interest.

text.text: The present synthesis cannot test this account, because assessment beyond the end of the intervention was uncommon.
Interventions raised competence beliefs (g = 0.09) across 28 samples, a smaller effect than for task value and mindset and comparable to that for interest.

Among the contributing trials, Dennehy and Dasgupta (2017) illustrate one route, in which competence beliefs were reinforced through social experiences signaling belonging and capability rather than through cognitive reframing alone.
text.formatted: Among the contributing trials, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Dennehy and Dasgupta (2017)</ref> illustrate one route, in which competence beliefs were reinforced through social experiences signaling belonging and capability rather than through cognitive reframing alone.

text.text: Cost and goals outcomes did not yield estimates distinguishable from zero (cost g = 0.04; goals g = 0.09; see Table 1).
text.formatted: Cost and goals outcomes did not yield estimates distinguishable from zero (cost g = 0.04; goals g = 0.09; see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: For cost, the 47 contributing effect sizes came from 15 samples, and the upper bound of the confidence interval reaches 0.10, so the null estimate is imprecise rather than tightly bounded.

Research beyond the sample suggests that perceived cost is tied to structural features of learning environments such as workload, competing demands and opportunity trade-offs, which reinterpretation alone may not alter, and that single-session interventions may not reach the in-the-moment cost perceptions most predictive of academic outcomes (Beymer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Research beyond the sample suggests that perceived cost is tied to structural features of learning environments such as workload, competing demands and opportunity trade-offs, which reinterpretation alone may not alter, and that single-session interventions may not reach the in-the-moment cost perceptions most predictive of academic outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Beymer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A further possibility is that activities asking students to reflect on costs make those costs more salient.

A rise in reported cost need not be maladaptive in that case, as higher perceived cost has not always been accompanied by lower performance in cost-focused trials (Rosenzweig et al., 2020; Rosenzweig et al., 2022).
text.formatted: A rise in reported cost need not be maladaptive in that case, as higher perceived cost has not always been accompanied by lower performance in cost-focused trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">(Rosenzweig et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Rosenzweig et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Although individual achievement goal orientations were coded at the subscale level, they were analyzed together as a single category because only six samples measured these outcomes.
The combined estimate was not statistically distinguishable from zero, but this does not establish that interventions have no effect on specific goal orientations.
Two explanations remain possible.

Goal orientations may be difficult to change through brief interventions because they are shaped by sustained classroom practices and evaluative climates (Guo et al., 2023), or different goal orientations may respond differently, with aggregation obscuring these differences.
text.formatted: Goal orientations may be difficult to change through brief interventions because they are shaped by sustained classroom practices and evaluative climates <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Guo et al., 2023)</ref>, or different goal orientations may respond differently, with aggregation obscuring these differences.

text.text: The present analysis cannot distinguish these explanations, highlighting the need for future studies to examine specific goal orientations separately.
Attributions showed the largest point estimate (g = 0.19), but it rests on three effect sizes from three samples, and its confidence interval is wide, so it is not interpreted here.
Attributional retraining has its own evidence base (e.g., Hamm et al., 2020) and merits a dedicated synthesis in STEM.
text.formatted: Attributional retraining has its own evidence base (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Hamm et al., 2020)</ref> and merits a dedicated synthesis in STEM.

text.text: This meta-analysis examined the effects of psychosocial interventions on measured motivational outcomes rather than the psychological mechanisms underlying these effects.
Differences across outcomes do not establish that changes in one motivational belief lead to changes in another.
For example, an effect on task value does not show that changes in task value account for the effects on interest or competence beliefs.

Moreover, because motivational outcomes were not assessed consistently across trials, differences between outcome categories may partly reflect variation in intervention content, samples, measures, or assessment timing.
Downstream outcomes, such as engagement, achievement, and STEM participation, were not examined.

Future research should directly test the proposed mechanisms, such as changes in how students interpret task relevance, competence, and challenge, using temporally ordered assessments of mediators and subsequent outcomes.

Intervention type did not significantly moderate effects, and the four intervention categories (task value, framing, personal values and combined) yielded similar estimates, ranging from g = 0.11 to 0.14.

However, the absence of statistically significant differences does not establish that these intervention types are equally effective or operate through common psychological mechanisms, and the confidence intervals around the type estimates are wide.
The categories are broad and do not capture differences in specific intervention components, implementation or assessment timing, and the combined category incorporates components of the other three.
The present analysis therefore cannot determine whether different intervention types operate through similar or distinct psychological processes.
Trials that compare intervention types head-to-head would be needed to test this.
Two participant characteristics were examined as sample-level moderators.
Neither sample gender composition nor the proportion of participants from groups underrepresented in STEM, available for 29 samples, was associated with intervention effects.

Girls and women face distinct motivational barriers in STEM contexts, including lower competence beliefs, higher perceived costs, and weaker identity alignment (Diekman et al., 2010; Eccles & Wigfield, 2024), but sample gender composition was not associated with intervention effects in the present data.
text.formatted: Girls and women face distinct motivational barriers in STEM contexts, including lower competence beliefs, higher perceived costs, and weaker identity alignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Diekman et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Eccles & Wigfield, 2024)</ref>, but sample gender composition was not associated with intervention effects in the present data.

text.text: The wider literature still offers a rationale for expecting such interventions to address these barriers.

Valueaffirmation activities can bolster students' sense of self-integrity and reduce defensive responses to evaluative threat (Harackiewicz et al., 2014), and utility-value interventions that help students connect STEM to personally meaningful or prosocial goals may counter narratives that STEM is irrelevant to their lives or incompatible with their values or identities.
text.formatted: Valueaffirmation activities can bolster students' sense of self-integrity and reduce defensive responses to evaluative threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Harackiewicz et al., 2014)</ref>, and utility-value interventions that help students connect STEM to personally meaningful or prosocial goals may counter narratives that STEM is irrelevant to their lives or incompatible with their values or identities.

text.text: The present synthesis provides no evidence for or against that account, and we report it as a rationale for direct testing rather than as an interpretation of our findings.

The analysis rests on sample-level proportions, so the null result also does not show that these interventions are equally effective for girls and women as for boys and men, and it is compatible with individual-level differences in either direction.
The null result for racial and ethnic composition does not establish that psychosocial interventions are differentially effective across samples with varying proportions of underrepresented students.
Furthermore, these study-level comparisons cannot determine whether individual students from underrepresented groups respond differently to intervention.

Sample-level composition may be an imperfect proxy for which students benefit from an intervention. Harackiewicz et al. (2023), reporting further on the chemistry trial that contributes effect sizes here as Asher et al. (2023), illustrate this.
text.formatted: Sample-level composition may be an imperfect proxy for which students benefit from an intervention. <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Harackiewicz et al. (2023)</ref>, reporting further on the chemistry trial that contributes effect sizes here as <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Asher et al. (2023)</ref>, illustrate this.

text.text: In that trial a version of the intervention emphasizing both personal and prosocial value benefited first-generation students mainly among those entering with higher confidence in their ability to succeed, and it did so both against the standard version of the intervention and against a no-intervention control.
That pattern is consistent with psychosocial interventions building on students' existing motivational resources rather than supplying them.

It was, however, specific to the chemistry course; in the companion biology study the benefit for first-generation students did not depend on confidence, so whether the pattern generalizes cannot be determined here.

This pattern does not support deficit-oriented interpretations of motivation among underrepresented groups and fits the view that intervention content must connect with students' existing motivations and contextual experiences to take effect.
The findings raise a broader theoretical question about how changes initiated by psychosocial interventions interact with the longer-term development of students' motivational beliefs.

The positive but modest average effect describes the interventions as implemented, which were often brief and evaluated at the end of the intervention or academic term, and does not by itself establish that motivational beliefs are resistant to change.

Although the outcomes examined originate in several theoretical traditions, SEVT provides a developmental perspective on expectancy and value beliefs, emphasizing how they are shaped by cumulative experiences at school, at home and in wider society (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: Although the outcomes examined originate in several theoretical traditions, SEVT provides a developmental perspective on expectancy and value beliefs, emphasizing how they are shaped by cumulative experiences at school, at home and in wider society <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal research has documented declines in mathematics and science competence beliefs and task values across the school years (Guo et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Longitudinal research has documented declines in mathematics and science competence beliefs and task values across the school years <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Guo et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Jacobs et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, a brief intervention is one influence among many, which may partly explain the modest average effect.
At the same time, initial changes may be sustained or amplified when subsequent experiences reinforce them (Yeager & Walton, 2011).
text.formatted: At the same time, initial changes may be sustained or amplified when subsequent experiences reinforce them <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Yeager & Walton, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Whether repeated, sustained or contextually embedded interventions (Linnenbrink-Garcia et al., 2026) produce larger and more enduring changes remains an open question requiring longer-term investigation.
text.formatted: Whether repeated, sustained or contextually embedded interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Linnenbrink-Garcia et al., 2026)</ref> produce larger and more enduring changes remains an open question requiring longer-term investigation.

text.text: Beyond establishing a small positive average effect, this synthesis identifies meaningful variation in intervention effects across motivational outcomes.
Motivational construct significantly moderated effects, whereas intervention type did not.

As these outcomes originate in different motivational theories, this variation suggests that understanding intervention effectiveness requires attention to the motivational outcomes being assessed, rather than intervention categories alone.

One possible theoretical explanation is that brief interventions most readily change beliefs that rest on students' situated interpretations of their learning experiences, such as the relevance of academic tasks or the malleability of ability, and less readily change beliefs tied to objective constraints, such as the competing demands that shape perceived cost.
This explanation is consistent with SEVT's emphasis on contextually shaped motivational beliefs, but it remains untested.
Differences across outcomes may also partly reflect differences between the contributing studies.
The role of students' situated interpretations also bears on equity, since how students interpret an intervention depends on the experiences and resources they bring to it.
Students from groups underrepresented in STEM should not be characterized solely in terms of the barriers they encounter.

The community cultural wealth framework recognizes the aspirational, linguistic, familial, social, navigational, and resistant capital that students from marginalized communities bring to educational settings (Yosso, 2005).
text.formatted: The community cultural wealth framework recognizes the aspirational, linguistic, familial, social, navigational, and resistant capital that students from marginalized communities bring to educational settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">(Yosso, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Institutional practices may not always recognize or support these resources (Stephens et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Institutional practices may not always recognize or support these resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">(Stephens et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, psychosocial interventions may be particularly meaningful when they connect STEM learning to students' existing values, aspirations, and cultural resources rather than assuming motivational deficits.

Related approaches include difference-education interventions for first-generation college students (Stephens et al., 2014) and utility-value interventions that emphasize prosocial and personal values (Harackiewicz et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Related approaches include difference-education interventions for first-generation college students <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">(Stephens et al., 2014)</ref> and utility-value interventions that emphasize prosocial and personal values <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Harackiewicz et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, such interventions do not themselves remove structural barriers, and their effectiveness may depend on the extent to which learning environments recognize and support the resources students bring.
Whether such designs produce larger or more enduring motivational gains for students from underrepresented groups than other approaches could not be tested in the present synthesis.
The present findings offer several tentative implications for practice.
First, when the goal is to improve students' perceived task value, mindset, interest, or competence beliefs, psychosocial interventions are a reasonable option.

When the priority is to reduce perceived cost or change achievement goal orientations, the evidence is less conclusive, so educators should evaluate whether these interventions produce the intended changes rather than assume comparable benefits.

Instructional approaches that provide opportunities for students to experience success, to treat errors as part of learning, and to connect STEM content to personally meaningful goals may support the same outcomes through routine practice rather than discrete activities (Y.-F. Lee et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Instructional approaches that provide opportunities for students to experience success, to treat errors as part of learning, and to connect STEM content to personally meaningful goals may support the same outcomes through routine practice rather than discrete activities (Y.-F. <ref type="bibr">Lee et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Psychosocial interventions are best understood not as standalone solutions but as one component of environments that support motivation through instruction, feedback and classroom culture.

Effects also did not differ across the broad intervention types examined, so effectiveness may depend less on selecting a particular type of program than on how well an intervention fits the context, population and barriers at hand, and on whether it is delivered so that students can engage with its content (reframing difficulty, articulating relevance or affirming values) as designed.
Second, interventions are likely to be most effective when they address the motivational barriers students actually experience.

For example, emphasizing the prosocial relevance of STEM may suit students whose motivations are closely tied to helping others (Harackiewicz et al., 2023; Shin et al., 2023), and strengthening competence beliefs may suit settings marked by low confidence or high evaluative pressure (e.g., Dennehy & Dasgupta, 2017).
text.formatted: For example, emphasizing the prosocial relevance of STEM may suit students whose motivations are closely tied to helping others <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Harackiewicz et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Shin et al., 2023)</ref>, and strengthening competence beliefs may suit settings marked by low confidence or high evaluative pressure (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Dennehy & Dasgupta, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The present synthesis provides no evidence that effects differ by sample gender composition or by the proportion of participants from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM.

Interventions for students from underrepresented groups should therefore be designed around the motivational needs of those students in their particular contexts, rather than assuming that a given approach will work better for them.
Several limitations qualify these findings.
First, the evidence base is narrow in scope.

Restricting inclusion to RCTs in STEM subjects strengthened internal validity but excluded potentially informative studies in adjacent domains, such as psychology courses (American Psychological Association, 2009).
text.formatted: Restricting inclusion to RCTs in STEM subjects strengthened internal validity but excluded potentially informative studies in adjacent domains, such as psychology courses <ref type="bibr">(American Psychological Association, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Most trials were conducted in the United States (37 of 52), which limits generalizability given SEVT's emphasis on sociocultural context; with few samples from other countries, the absence of country moderation should not be read as evidence that interventions are equally effective across cultural contexts.

The studies also span 2009 to 2026, a period in which constructs such as perceived cost came to be measured more finely; publication year is too coarse an indicator to establish that constructs were defined or measured consistently over time.
Second, the construct categories limit what comparisons across outcomes can show.
Attributions yielded three effect sizes, and mindset rests on 11 effect sizes from six samples.

Competence, interest and task value each aggregate theoretically separable constructs, because the primary studies do not distinguish them consistently and finer categories would have been too sparse; estimates within these categories may average over constructs on which effects differ, and the null result for goals is consistent with mastery and performance orientations moving in opposite directions.
Comparisons between categories are also partly confounded with differences between the contributing studies.

Forty of the 52 samples assessed more than one category, so part of each comparison is made within studies, but the combinations varied, and the studies behind each category differed in intervention content, comparison conditions, participants, measures and timing of assessment.

Intervention type was coded, but its four broad categories cannot separate specific intervention components or implementation features from the construct itself, and duration and delivery format, which were also examined, are confounded with intervention type and education setting.
A larger effect for one category therefore cannot be attributed to the construct alone.
More definitive comparisons require trials that measure several constructs in the same sample with comparable measures, and finer coding of intervention components across trials.
Third, study quality and reporting limit confidence in the estimates.
Thirty-two of the 52 samples were rated at high risk of bias and only three at low risk; the pooled effect remained positive without the high-risk samples, but less precisely estimated.
In classroom trials, blinding of students and teachers is rarely possible and attrition is common, so the high overall ratings partly reflect the setting rather than the conduct of individual trials.

Bayesian selection models strongly favored the absence of p-value-based selection and gave an adjusted estimate close to the primary one, but because these models assess selection at the level of the effect size and the Egger slope was positive, some small-study bias cannot be fully excluded.

Inconsistent reporting also required some results to be reconstructed, and nine of the 17 cluster-randomized trials had no reported or computable intraclass correlation, so their design-effect corrections rest on imputed values for eight trials and on a value from a closely related trial for one.
Fourth, the moderator findings are provisional and study-level.

No included trial randomly assigned duration, and duration is confounded with intervention type, education setting and delivery format, so its association with effect size should not be read as evidence that lengthening an intervention would increase its effect.
Implementation details such as facilitator characteristics, teacher training and fidelity monitoring were often unreported, so the conditions under which the estimates apply are frequently unclear.

Large trials often deliver interventions through regular instruction or online platforms with limited tailoring and monitoring, so the pooled estimate may partly reflect these implementation conditions rather than the potential of more intensively supported delivery.

Finally, the evidence base constrains what can be established about equity, although the promise of these interventions for students underrepresented in STEM is among the most common justifications for them.

Twenty-three of the 52 samples did not report racial or ethnic composition in a form permitting computation, and those that did were all conducted in the United States; the included trials contained no samples from England, Canada, or Australia, and the one sample from New Zealand, where ethnicity data are routinely collected, did not provide usable ethnicity data.
Future trials should collect and report students' racial and ethnic background, using categories appropriate to their national context, and family income, in the United States and elsewhere.
No study reported socioeconomic indicators in a form that permitted comparison.

The lack of socioeconomic information matters particularly for perceived cost, because some barriers to STEM participation reflect material circumstances that psychosocial interventions alone cannot resolve; this may help explain the limited effects on cost but could not be examined.

Composition was available only at the sample level, so the analyses show whether effects differ across samples rather than whether individual students respond differently, and they cannot identify effects for intersecting groups.

Gender composition and the proportion of participants from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM were uncorrelated across the 29 samples reporting both (r = -.01), but this says nothing about how they overlap within individuals.
Most studies also reported gender in binary categories without specifying whether sex or gender identity was measured, and nonbinary participants, where reported, were too few to analyze separately.

Primary trials should report effects separately by student background, with the descriptive statistics needed to compute effect sizes, and describe how gender was assessed, with options beyond binary categories.
This meta-analysis provides evidence that psychosocial interventions can improve students' STEM motivation, although the overall effect is small.

The largest effects were observed for task value and mindset, with smaller but significant effects on interest and competence beliefs, whereas effects on cost and goals were not statistically significant.
Intervention effects did not differ significantly by sample gender composition or the proportion of participants from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in STEM.
Overall, these findings indicate that psychosocial interventions can modestly strengthen students' STEM motivation, particularly their perceptions of STEM's value.
Whether these gains last beyond the end of an intervention and lead to sustained STEM engagement and participation remains to be tested.

; (v) include interventions that target a primary psychosocial component relating to motivation, such as task value, framing or personal values; (vi) be conducted in educational settings either in face-to-face or online capacities; (vii) randomly assign students or groups of students to experimental and comparison groups (control or alternate intervention); and (viii) be situated in a STEM subject domain, defined as science (including physics, chemistry, and biology), mathematics (including applied, advanced, foundation mathematics, and calculus), technology (including digital technology), or engineering.
This definition was used to guide eligibility screening and does not imply that the included motivational constructs are theoretically equivalent.

Studies were excluded if they (i) used qualitative methodologies; (ii) did not present original data (e.g., previous reviews and meta-analyses); (iii) included students enrolled in preschool settings; (iv) did not examine students' motivational constructs in relation to STEM subjects; (v) did not have an intervention that primarily involved a psychosocial component relating to motivation; (vi) were not conducted in an educational setting (e.g., a community-based program, or research conducted in a laboratory not associated with an educational setting); (vii) did not randomly assign students or groups of students to experimental and comparison groups; or (viii) students were not participating in STEM subjects.
